primer.text: Every moving object carries a stored 'quantity of motion' that grows with both its mass and its speed. That single idea explains why a small, fast ball can land as hard as a slow, heavy truck. This note names the quantity, builds its equation, and then follows it unchanged through every collision and explosion.

modules.title: Calculating momentum
sourceHeadings: How does the momentum of a ball change after a collision?
modules.opening: Picture a tennis ball flying at full speed and a heavy brick strolling along — which one is harder to stop? Physics answers with a single quantity that combines mass and velocity. In this lesson you give that quantity a name, a unit and an equation, and learn why its sign tracks direction.
keyPoints: Momentum belongs to every moving object, and it is worked out by multiplying mass by velocity: p = m × v.
Momentum is measured in kilogram metres per second (kg m/s), mass in kilograms and velocity in metres per second.
A stationary object has zero velocity, so it carries no momentum at all.
Because velocity is a vector, momentum depends on travel direction and can be positive or negative.
With the usual sign choice, motion to the right counts as positive and motion to the left counts as negative.
A large momentum makes an object stubborn: hard to slow down or steer onto a new path.

low.restatement: Momentum is just mass multiplied by velocity — a signed number saying how much motion an object carries and which way it goes.
low.analogy: Think of a shopping trolley: mass is how much you loaded, velocity is how fast you push it, and momentum is the product stamped on the receipt.
low.examPointer: Write momentum's unit as kg m/s — exactly the mass unit times the velocity unit.

medium.restatement: The vector side does the real work: velocity carries a direction, so momentum does too, which is why opposite journeys get opposite signs and can cancel.
medium.analogy: Picture momentum as money on a number line — rightward travel is credit, leftward travel is debt, and equal amounts wipe out.
medium.examPointer: Exams leave the positive direction to you; declare it once ('right is positive') and keep every velocity's sign consistent with it.

modules.title: Conservation of momentum
sourceHeadings: Conservation of momentum before and after a collision
modules.opening: Roll one trolley into another and the momentum they share afterwards is exactly the momentum they had before. That bookkeeping rule — total in equals total out — lets you predict masses and velocities you never measured. This lesson turns the rule into equations you can solve.
keyPoints: Conservation of momentum means the total before an interaction equals the total after it, provided no external forces act.
Collisions and explosions are the two interactions the rule covers.
In a two-object collision, the momentum before equals the momentum after, even though each object's own share changes.
After a rebound, the bounced-back object's velocity turns negative, so its term joins the total with a minus sign.
Because momentum is a vector, two objects moving oppositely at the same speed cancel, giving an overall momentum of zero.
A stationary object contributes nothing to the total because its momentum is zero.

low.restatement: Add up every object's momentum before a crash and again afterwards — the two totals match exactly.
low.analogy: Momentum behaves like marbles swapped between jars: the jars can end up holding different amounts, but the table still holds every marble.
low.examPointer: Questions usually ask for a speed — a size alone — so finish by dropping the sign once the algebra is done.

medium.restatement: Signs carry the physics: anything that reverses direction contributes a negative term, so totals are added algebraically, never by size alone.
medium.analogy: Treat each momentum as a signed entry in a shared ledger — every collision reshuffles the balances while the ledger's grand total never moves.
medium.examPointer: Sketch the before-and-after picture with an arrow for every velocity; that is what keeps masses and directions straight in conservation questions.

glossary.definition: A property of every moving object, equal to its mass multiplied by its velocity; a vector measured in kg m/s.
An object's speed together with its direction of travel.
A quantity that carries both a size and a direction.
The rule that, with no outside forces interfering, a system's total momentum before an interaction matches its total afterwards.
An interaction in which moving objects run into one another.
An interaction in which a body splits into two or more parts that fly apart.

workedExample.prompt: The diagram shows a tennis ball and a brick, each labelled with its mass and velocity. Decide which object has the greater momentum, and justify your choice.
steps: Read the values from the diagram: the tennis ball has mass 0.06 kg and velocity 75 m/s; the brick has mass 3 kg and velocity 1.5 m/s.
Tennis ball: p = m × v = 0.06 × 75 = 4.5 kg m/s.
Brick: p = m × v = 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 kg m/s.
Compare the two results: they are equal, so neither object wins — the brick's much larger mass is exactly offset by the ball's much larger speed.
At impact each delivers a comparable push — how large depends on how quickly each is brought to rest.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The two objects share the same momentum, 4.5 kg m/s: the ball's higher speed compensates for the brick's greater mass.
